entries.472a358957da05e4128d2431009f344a4a2bb37f: <div sID="gen19594" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Dan.11" sID="Dan.11"/> <div eID="gen19594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19595" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19596" type="x-p"/> The angel Gabriel, in this chapter, performs his promise made to Daniel in the foregoing chapter, that he would "show him what should befal his people in the latter days," according to that which was "written in the scriptures of truth:" very particularly does he here foretel the succession of the kings of Persia and Grecia, and the affairs of their kingdoms, especially the mischief which Antiochus Epiphanes did in his time to the church, which was foretold before (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.11-Dan.8.12">ch. viii. 11-12</reference>). Here is, I. A brief prediction of the setting up of the Grecian monarchy upon the ruins of the Persian monarchy, which was now newly begun, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.1-Dan.11.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. A prediction of the affairs of the two kingdoms of Egypt and Syria, with reference to each other, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.5-Dan.11.20">ver. 5-20</reference>. III. Of the rise of Antiochus Epiphanes, and his actions and successes, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.21-Dan.11.29">ver. 21-29</reference>. IV. Of the great mischief that he should do to the Jewish nation and religion, and his contempt of all religion, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30-Dan.11.39">ver. 30-39</reference>. V. Of his fall and ruin at last, when he is in the heat of his pursuit, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.40-Dan.11.45">ver. 40-45</reference>.
entries.ef92447b8586e8954491e68c85551358aec05e70: <div eID="gen19596" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19595" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ruin of the Persian Monarchy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 534.)</title> <div sID="gen19597" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Also I in the first year of Darius the Mede, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I, stood to confirm and to strengthen him. <hi type="super">2</hi> And now will I show thee the truth. Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than <hi type="italic">they</hi> all: and by his strength through his riches he shall stir up all against the realm of Grecia. <hi type="super">3</hi> And a mighty king shall stand up, that shall rule with great dominion, and do according to his will. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when he shall stand up, his kingdom shall be broken, and shall be divided toward the four winds of heaven; and not to his posterity, nor according to his dominion which he ruled: for his kingdom shall be plucked up, even for others beside those. <div eID="gen19597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19598" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The angel Gabriel lets Daniel know the good service he has done to the Jewish nation (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">In the first year of Darius the Mede,</hi> who destroyed Babylon and released the Jews out of that house of bondage, <hi type="italic">I stood a strength and fortress to him,</hi> that is, I was instrumental to protect him, and give him success in his ward, and, after he had conquered Babylon, to confirm him in his resolution to release the Jews," which, it is likely, met with much opposition. Thus by the angel, and at the request of <hi type="italic">the watcher,</hi> the golden head was broken, and the axe laid to the root of the tree. Note, We must acknowledge the hand of God in the strengthening of those that are friends to the church for the service they are to do it, and confirming them in their good resolutions; herein he uses the ministry of angels more than we are aware of. And the many instances we have known of God's care of his church formerly encourage us to depend upon him in further straits and difficulties. 2. He foretels the reign of four Persian kings (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now I will tell thee the truth,</hi> that is, the true meaning of the visions of the great image, and of the four beasts, and expound in plain terms what was before represented by dark types. (1.) There shall stand up <hi type="italic">three kings in Persia,</hi> besides Darius, in whose reign this prophecy is dated, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.1">ch. ix. 1</reference>. Mr. Broughton makes these three to be Cyrus, Artaxasta or Artaxerxes, called by the Greeks <hi type="italic">Cambyses,</hi> and Ahasuerus that married Esther, called <hi type="italic">Darius son of Hystaspes.</hi> To these three the Persians gave these attributes—Cyrus was a father, Cambyses a master, and Darius a hoarder up. So Herodotus. (2.) There shall be a fourth, <hi type="italic">far richer than they all,</hi> that is, Xerxes, of whose wealth the Greek authors take notice. By <hi type="italic">his strength</hi> (his vast army, consisting of 800,000 men at least) and <hi type="italic">his riches,</hi> with which he maintained and paid that vast army, he <hi type="italic">stirred up all</hi> against <hi type="italic">the realm of Greece.</hi> Xerxes's expedition against Greece is famous in history, and the shameful defeat that he met with. He who when he went out was the terror of Greece, in his return was the scorn of Greece. Daniel needed not to be told what disappointment he would meet with, for he was a hinderer of the building of the temple; but soon after, about thirty years after the first return from captivity, Darius, a young king, revived the building of the temple, owning the hand of God against his predecessors for hindering it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.7">Ezra vi. 7</reference>. 3. He foretels Alexander's conquests and the partition of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.3">v. 3</reference>. He is that <hi type="italic">mighty king</hi> that shall <hi type="italic">stand up</hi> against the kings of Persia, and he shall <hi type="italic">rule with great dominion,</hi> over many kingdoms, and with a despotic power, for he shall <hi type="italic">do according to his will,</hi> and undo likewise, which, by the law of the Medes and Persians, their kings could not. When Alexander, after he had conquered Asia, would be worshipped as a god, then this was fulfilled, that he shall <hi type="italic">do according to his will.</hi> That is God's prerogative, but was his pretension. But (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.4">v. 4</reference>) his <hi type="italic">kingdom</hi> shall soon be <hi type="italic">broken,</hi> and <hi type="italic">divided</hi> into four parts, <hi type="italic">but not to his posterity,</hi> nor shall any of his successors reign <hi type="italic">according to his dominion;</hi> none of them shall have such large territories nor such an absolute power. His <hi type="italic">kingdom was plucked up for others besides those</hi> of his own family. Arideus, his brother, was made king in Macedonia; Olympias, Alexander's mother, killed him, and poisoned Alexander's two sons, Hercules and Alexander. Thus was his family rooted out by its own hands. See what decaying perishing things worldly pomp and possessions are, and the powers by which they are got. Never was the vanity of the world and its greatest things shown more evidently than in the story of Alexander. <hi type="italic">All is vanity and vexation of spirit.</hi>
entries.953a8fb13f371969300f6700bf3fdd8893944918: <div eID="gen19598" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Affairs of Egypt and Syria; The Reign of Antiochus Magnus; The Fall of Antiochus Magnus. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  534.)</title> <div sID="gen19599" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And the king of the south shall be strong, and <hi type="italic">one</hi> of his princes; and he shall be strong above him, and have dominion; his dominion <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a great dominion. <hi type="super">6</hi> And in the end of years they shall join themselves together; for the king's daughter of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement: but she shall not retain the power of the arm; neither shall he stand, nor his arm: but she shall be given up, and they that brought her, and he that begat her, and he that strengthened her in <hi type="italic">these</hi> times. <hi type="super">7</hi> But out of a branch of her roots shall <hi type="italic">one</hi> stand up in his estate, which shall come with an army, and shall enter into the fortress of the king of the north, and shall deal against them, and shall prevail: <hi type="super">8</hi> And shall also carry captives into Egypt their gods, with their princes, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with their precious vessels of silver and of gold; and he shall continue <hi type="italic">more</hi> years than the king of the north. <hi type="super">9</hi> So the king of the south shall come into <hi type="italic">his</hi> kingdom, and shall return into his own land. <hi type="super">10</hi> But his sons shall be stirred up, and shall assemble a multitude of great forces: and <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall certainly come, and overflow, and pass through: then shall he return, and be stirred up, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to his fortress. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, <hi type="italic">even</hi> with the king of the north: and he shall set forth a great multitude; but the multitude shall be given into his hand. <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">And</hi> when he hath taken away the multitude, his heart shall be lifted up; and he shall cast down <hi type="italic">many</hi> ten thousands: but he shall not be strengthened <hi type="italic">by it.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> For the king of the north shall return, and shall set forth a multitude greater than the former, and shall certainly come after certain years with a great army and with much riches. <hi type="super">14</hi> And in those times there shall many stand up against the king of the south: also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; but they shall fall. <hi type="super">15</hi> So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither <hi type="italic">shall there be any</hi> strength to withstand. <hi type="super">16</hi> But he that cometh against him shall do according to his own will, and none shall stand before him: and he shall stand in the glorious land, which by his hand shall be consumed. <hi type="super">17</hi> He shall also set his face to enter with the strength of his whole kingdom, and upright ones with him; thus shall he do: and he shall give him the daughter of women, corrupting her: but she shall not stand <hi type="italic">on his side,</hi> neither be for him. <hi type="super">18</hi> After this shall he turn his face unto the isles, and shall take many: but a prince for his own behalf shall cause the reproach offered by him to cease; without his own reproach he shall cause <hi type="italic">it</hi> to turn upon him. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then he shall turn his face toward the fort of his own land: but he shall stumble and fall, and not be found. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then shall stand up in his estate a raiser of taxes <hi type="italic">in</hi> the glory of the kingdom: but within few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger, nor in battle. <div eID="gen19599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19600" type="x-p"/> Here are foretold, <div eID="gen19600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19601" type="x-p"/> I. The rise and power of two great kingdoms out of the remains of Alexander's conquests, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.5">v. 5</reference>. 1. The kingdom of Egypt, which was made considerable by Ptolemæus Lagus, one of Alexander's captains, whose successors were, from him, called the <hi type="italic">Lagidæ.</hi> He is called the king of the <hi type="italic">south,</hi> that is, Egypt, named here, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.42">42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.43">43</reference>. The countries that at first belonged to Ptolemy are reckoned to be Egypt, Phœnicia, Arabia, Libya, Ethiopia, &c. Theocr. Idyl. 17. 2. The kingdom of Syria, which was set up by Seleucus Nicanor, or the <hi type="italic">conqueror;</hi> he was one of Alexander's princes, and became stronger than the other, and <hi type="italic">had the greatest dominion of all,</hi> was the most powerful of all Alexander's successors. It was said that he had no fewer than seven-two kingdoms under him. Both these were strong against Judah (the affairs of which are particularly eyed in this prediction); Ptolemy, soon after he gained Egypt, invaded Judea, and took Jerusalem <hi type="italic">on a sabbath,</hi> pretending a friendly visit. Seleucus also gave disturbance to Judea. <div eID="gen19601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19602" type="x-p"/> II. The fruitless attempt to unite these two kingdoms as iron and clay in Nebuchadnezzar's image (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">At the end of certain years,</hi> about seventy after Alexander's death, the Lagidæ and the Seleucidæ shall associate, but not in sincerity. Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, shall marry his daughter Berenice to Antiochus Theos, king of Syria," who had already a wife called <hi type="italic">Laodice.</hi> "Berenice shall come to the <hi type="italic">king of the north,</hi> to make an agreement, but it shall not hold: <hi type="italic">She shall not retain the power of the arm;</hi> neither she nor her posterity shall establish themselves in the kingdom of the north, neither shall Ptolemy her father, nor Antiochus her husband (between whom there was to be a great alliance), <hi type="italic">stand,</hi> nor their arm, but <hi type="italic">she shall be given up and those that brought her,</hi>" all that projected that unhappy marriage between her and Antiochus, which occasioned so much mischief, instead of producing a coalition between the northern and southern crowns, as was hoped. Antiochus divorced Berenice, took his former wife Laodice again, who soon after poisoned him, procured Berenice and her son to be murdered, and set up her own son by Antiochus to be king, who was called <hi type="italic">Seleucus Callinicus.</hi> <div eID="gen19602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19603" type="x-p"/> III. A war between the two kingdoms, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.7-Dan.11.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. A branch from the same root with Berenice <hi type="italic">shall stand up in his estate.</hi> Ptolemæus Euergetes, the son and successor of Ptolemæus Philadelphus, shall come with an army against Seleucus Callinicus, king of Syria, to avenge his sister's quarrel, and shall prevail; and he shall carry away a rich booty both of persons and goods into Egypt, and shall <hi type="italic">continue more years than the king of the north.</hi> This Ptolemy reigned forty-six years; and Justin says that if his own affairs had not called him home he would, in this war, have made himself master of the whole kingdom of Syria. But (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.9">v. 9</reference>) he shall be forced to <hi type="italic">come into his kingdom</hi> and <hi type="italic">return into his own land,</hi> to keep peace there, so that he can no longer carry on the war abroad. Note, It is very common for a treacherous peace to end in a bloody war. <div eID="gen19603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19604" type="x-p"/> IV. The long and busy reign of <hi type="italic">Antiochus the Great,</hi> king of Syria. Seleucus Callinicus, that king of the north that was overcome (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.7">v. 7</reference>) and died miserably, left two sons, Seleucus and Antiochus; these are his sons, the sons of the <hi type="italic">king of the north,</hi> that shall be <hi type="italic">stirred up, and shall assemble a multitude of great forces,</hi> to recover what their father had lost, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.10">v. 10</reference>. But Seleucus the elder, being weak, and unable to rule his army, was poisoned by his friends, and reigned only two years; and his brother Antiochus succeeded him, who reigned thirty-seven years, and was called <hi type="italic">the Great.</hi> And therefore the angel, though he speaks of <hi type="italic">sons</hi> at first, goes on with the account of <hi type="italic">one only,</hi> who was but fifteen years old when he began to reign, and he shall <hi type="italic">certainly come, and overflow,</hi> and <hi type="italic">over-run,</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">be restored</hi> at length to what his father lost. 1. The <hi type="italic">king of the south,</hi> in this war, shall at first have very great success. Ptolemæus Philopater, moved with indignation at the indignities done by <hi type="italic">Antiochus the Great,</hi> shall (though otherwise a slothful prince) <hi type="italic">come forth, and fight with him,</hi> and shall bring a vast army into the field of 70,000 foot, and 5000 horse, and seventy-three elephants. And the <hi type="italic">other multitude</hi> (the army of Antiochus, consisting of 62,000 foot, and 6000 horse, and 102 elephants) shall <hi type="italic">be given into his hand.</hi> Polybius, who lived with Scipio, has given a particular account of this battle of Raphia. Ptolemæus Philopater, having gained this victory, grew very insolent; <hi type="italic">his heart was lifted up;</hi> then he went into the temple of God at Jerusalem, and, in defiance of the law, entered the most holy place, for which God has a controversy with him, so that, though he shall <hi type="italic">cast down many myriads,</hi> yet he shall <hi type="italic">not be strengthened by it,</hi> so as to secure his interest. For, 2. The <hi type="italic">king of the north, Antiochus the Great,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">return</hi> with a <hi type="italic">greater army</hi> than <hi type="italic">the former;</hi> and, at the <hi type="italic">end of times (that is, years</hi>) he shall <hi type="italic">come with a mighty army, and great riches,</hi> against the <hi type="italic">king of the south,</hi> that is, Ptolemæus Epiphanes, who succeeded Ptolemæus Philopater his father, when he was a child, which gave advantage to Antiochus the Great. In this expedition he had some powerful allies (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many shall stand up against the king of the south.</hi> Philip of Macedon was confederate with Antiochus against the king of Egypt, and Scopas his general, whom he sent into Syria; Antiochus routed him, destroyed a great part of his army; whereupon the Jews willingly yielded to Antiochus, joined with him, helped him to besiege Ptolemæus's garrisons. They <hi type="italic">the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision,</hi> to help forward the accomplishment of this prophecy; but <hi type="italic">they shall fall, and shall come to nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">v. 14</reference>. Hereupon (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.15">v. 15</reference>) the <hi type="italic">king of the north,</hi> this same Antiochus Magnus, shall carry on his design against the king of the south another way. (1.) He shall surprise his strong-holds; all that he has got in Syria and Samaria, and the arms of the south, all the power of the king of Egypt, shall not be able to withstand him. See how dubious and variable the turns of the scale of war are; like buying and selling, it is winning and losing; sometimes one side gets the better and sometimes the other; yet neither by chance; it is not, as they call it, the <hi type="italic">fortune of war,</hi> but according to the will and counsel of God, who brings some low and raises others up. (2.) He shall make himself master of the land of Judea (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that comes against him</hi> (that is, the king of the north) shall carry all before him and do what he pleases, and <hi type="italic">he shall stand</hi> and get footing <hi type="italic">in the glorious land;</hi> so the land of Israel was, and <hi type="italic">by his hand</hi> it was wasted and consumed, for with the spoil of that good land he victualled his vast army. The land of Judea lay between these two potent kingdoms of Egypt and Syria, so that in all the struggles between them that was sure to suffer, for to it they both bore <hi type="italic">ill will.</hi> Yet some read this, <hi type="italic">By his hand it shall be perfected;</hi> as if it intimated that the land of Judea, being taken under the protection of this Antiochus, shall flourish, and be in better condition than it had been. (3.) He shall still push on his war against the king of Egypt, and <hi type="italic">set his face</hi> to <hi type="italic">enter with the strength of his whole kingdom,</hi> taking advantage of the infancy of Ptolemy Epiphanes, and the <hi type="italic">upright ones,</hi> many of the pious Israelites, siding with him, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.17">v. 17</reference>. In prosecution of his design, he shall give him his daughter Cleopatra to wife, designing, as Saul in giving his daughter Cleopatra to David, that she should be a <hi type="italic">snare to him,</hi> and do him a mischief; but she <hi type="italic">shall not stand on her father's</hi> side, nor be <hi type="italic">for him,</hi> but for her husband, and so that plot failed him. (4.) His war with the Romans is here foretold (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.18">v. 18</reference>): He shall <hi type="italic">turn his face to the isles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.18">v. 18</reference>), the isles of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen. x. 5</reference>), Greece and Italy. He took many of the isles about the Hellespont-Rhodes, Samos, Delos, &c., which by war or treaty he made himself master of; but a <hi type="italic">prince,</hi> or <hi type="italic">state</hi> (so some), even the Roman senate, or a <hi type="italic">leader,</hi> even the Roman general, shall <hi type="italic">return his reproach</hi> with which he abused the Romans <hi type="italic">upon himself,</hi> or shall <hi type="italic">make his shame rest on himself,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without his own shame,</hi> or any disgrace to himself, shall <hi type="italic">pay him again.</hi> This was fulfilled when the two Scipios were sent with an army against Antiochus. Hannibal was then with him, and advised him to invade Italy and waste it as he had done; but he did not take his advice; and Scipio joined battle with him, and gave him a total defeat, though Antiochus had 70,000 men and the Romans but 30 000. Thus he caused the <hi type="italic">reproach offered by him to cease.</hi> (5.) His fall. When he was totally routed by the Romans, and was forced to abandon to them all he had in Europe, and had a very heavy tribute exacted from him, he <hi type="italic">turned to his own land,</hi> and, not knowing which way to raise money to pay his tribute, he plundered a temple of Jupiter, which so incensed his own subjects against him that they set upon him, and killed him; so he was overthrown, and <hi type="italic">fell,</hi> and <hi type="italic">was no more found,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.19">v. 19</reference>. (6.) His next successor, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.20">v. 20</reference>. There rose up one in his place, a <hi type="italic">raiser of taxes,</hi> a <hi type="italic">sender forth of the extortioner,</hi> or extorter. This character was remarkably answered in Seleucus Philopater, the elder son of Antiochus the Great, who was a great oppressor of his own subjects, and exacted abundance of money from them; and, when he was told he would thereby lose his friends, he said he knew no better friend he had than <hi type="italic">money.</hi> He likewise attempted to rob the temple at Jerusalem, which this seems especially to refer to. But <hi type="italic">within a few days he shall be destroyed, neither in anger nor in battle,</hi> but poisoned by Heliodorus, one of his own servants, when he had reigned but twelve years, and done nothing remarkable. <div eID="gen19604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19605" type="x-p"/> V. From all this let us learn, 1. That God in his providence sets up one, and pulls down another, as he pleases, advances some from low beginnings and depresses others that were very high. Some have called great men the <hi type="italic">foot-balls of fortune;</hi> or, rather, they are the <hi type="italic">tools of Providence.</hi> 2. This world is full of <hi type="italic">wars and fightings,</hi> which come <hi type="italic">from men's lusts,</hi> and make it a theatre of sin and misery. 3. All the changes and revolutions of states and kingdoms, and every event, even the most minute and contingent, were plainly and perfectly foreseen by the God of heaven, and to him nothing is <hi type="italic">new.</hi> 4. No word of God shall fall to the ground; but what he has designed, what he has declared, shall infallibly come to pass; and even the sins of men shall be made to serve his purpose, and contribute to the b ringing of his counsels to birth in their season; and yet <hi type="italic">God is not the author of sin.</hi> 5. That, for the right understanding of some parts of scripture, it is necessary that heathen authors be consulted, which give light to the scripture, and show the accomplishment of what is there foretold; we have therefore reason to bless God for the human learning with which many have done great service to divine truths.
entries.7947a8533b34a7614aa257dd06f9eab576db3dcc: <div eID="gen19605" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reign of Antiochus Epiphanes; Cruelty and Impiety of Antiochus; The Death of Antiochus. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  534.)</title> <div sID="gen19606" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries. <hi type="super">22</hi> And with the arms of a flood shall they be overflown from before him, and shall be broken; yea, also the prince of the covenant. <hi type="super">23</hi> And after the league <hi type="italic">made</hi> with him he shall work deceitfully: for he shall come up, and shall become strong with a small people. <hi type="super">24</hi> He shall enter peaceably even upon the fattest places of the province; and he shall do <hi type="italic">that</hi> which his fathers have not done, nor his fathers' fathers; he shall scatter among them the prey, and spoil, and riches: <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> and he shall forecast his devices against the strong holds, even for a time. <hi type="super">25</hi> And he shall stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south shall be stirred up to battle with a very great and mighty army; but he shall not stand: for they shall forecast devices against him. <hi type="super">26</hi> Yea, they that feed of the portion of his meat shall destroy him, and his army shall overflow: and many shall fall down slain. <hi type="super">27</hi> And both these kings' hearts <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table; but it shall not prosper: for yet the end <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> at the time appointed. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then shall he return into his land with great riches; and his heart <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> against the holy covenant; and he shall do <hi type="italic">exploits,</hi> and return to his own land. <hi type="super">29</hi> At the time appointed he shall return, and come toward the south; but it shall not be as the former, or as the latter. <hi type="super">30</hi> For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall be grieved, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; What troubles the Jews met with in the reigns of the Persian kings were not so particularly foretold to Daniel as these, because then they had living prophets with them, Haggai and Zechariah, to encourage them; but these troubles in the days of Antiochus were foretold, because, before that time, prophecy would cease, and they would find it necessary to have recourse to the written word. Some things in this prediction concerning Antiochus are alluded to in the New-Testament predictions of the antichrist, especially <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36-Dan.11.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. And as it is usual with the prophets, when they foretel the prosperity of the Jewish church, to make use of such expressions as were applicable to the <hi type="italic">kingdom of Christ,</hi> and insensibly to slide into a prophecy of that, so, when they foretel the troubles of the church, they make use of such expressions as have a further reference to the kingdom of the antichrist, the rise and ruin of that. Now concerning Antiochus, the angel foretels here, <div eID="gen19607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19608" type="x-p"/> I. His character: He shall be a <hi type="italic">vile person.</hi> He called himself <hi type="italic">Epiphanes—the illustrious,</hi> but his character was the reverse of his surname. The heathen writers describe him to be an <hi type="italic">odd-humoured</hi> man, rude and boisterous, base and sordid. He would sometimes steal out of the court into the city, and herd with any infamous company <hi type="italic">incognito—in disguise</hi> he made himself a companion of the common sort, and of the basest strangers that came to town. He had the most unaccountable whims, so that some took him to be silly, others to be mad. Hence he was called <hi type="italic">Epimanes—the madman.</hi> He is called a <hi type="italic">vile person,</hi> for he had been a long time a hostage at Rome for the fidelity of his father when the Romans had subdued him; and it was agreed that, when the other hostages were exchanged, he should continue a prisoner at large. <div eID="gen19608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19609" type="x-p"/> II. His accession to the crown. By a trick he got his elder brother's son, Demetrius, to be sent a hostage to Rome, in exchange for him, contrary to the cartel; and, his elder brother being made away with by Heliodorus (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.20">v. 20</reference>), he took the kingdom. The states of Syria did not <hi type="italic">give it</hi> to <hi type="italic">him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.21">v. 21</reference>), because they knew it belonged to his elder brother's son, nor did he get it by the sword, but <hi type="italic">came in peaceably,</hi> pretending to reign for his brother's son, Demetrius, then a hostage at Rome. But with the help of Eumenes and Attalus, neighbouring princes, he gained an interest in the people, and <hi type="italic">by flatteries obtained the kingdom,</hi> established himself in it, and crushed Heliodorus, who made head against him <hi type="italic">with the arms of a flood;</hi> those that opposed him were <hi type="italic">overflown</hi> and <hi type="italic">broken before him,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the prince of the covenant,</hi> his nephew, the rightful heir, whom he pretended to covenant with that he would resign to him whenever he should return, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.22">v. 22</reference>. But (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.23">v. 23</reference>) <hi type="italic">after the league made with him he shall work deceitfully,</hi> as one whose avowed maxim it is that princes ought not to be bound by their word any longer than it is for their interest. And <hi type="italic">with a small people,</hi> that at first cleave to him, he shall <hi type="italic">become strong,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.24">v. 24</reference>) <hi type="italic">he shall enter peaceably upon the fattest places</hi> of the kingdom of Syria, and, very unlike his predecessors, shall <hi type="italic">scatter</hi> among the people the <hi type="italic">prey, and the spoil, and riches,</hi> to insinuate himself into their affections; but, at the same time, he shall <hi type="italic">forecast his devices against the strong-holds,</hi> to make himself master of them, so that his generosity shall last but for a time; when he has got the garrisons into his hands he will scatter his spoil no more, but rule by force, as those commonly do that come in by fraud. He that comes in like a fox reigns like a lion. Some understand <reference osisRef="Dan.11.21-Dan.11.35">these verses</reference> of his first expedition into Egypt, when he came not as an enemy, but as a friend and guardian to the young king Ptolemæus Philometer, and therefore brought with him but few followers, yet those stout men, and faithful to his interest, whom he placed in divers of the strong-holds in Egypt, thereby making himself master of them. <div eID="gen19609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19610" type="x-p"/> III. His war with Egypt, which was his second expedition thither. This is described, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.25">v. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.27">27</reference>. Antiochus shall <hi type="italic">stir up his power and courage</hi> against Ptolemæus Philometer king of Egypt. After the battle, a treaty of peace shall be set on foot, and these two kings shall meet <hi type="italic">at one council-board,</hi> to adjust the articles of peace between them; but they shall neither of them be sincere in it, for they shall, in their pretences and promises of amity and friendship, <hi type="italic">lie to one another,</hi> for their hearts shall be at the same time to do one another all the mischief they can. And then no marvel that <hi type="italic">it shall not prosper.</hi> The peace shall not last; but <hi type="italic">the end</hi> of it shall be <hi type="italic">at the time appointed</hi> in the divine Providence, and then the war shall break out again, as a sore that is only skinned over. <div eID="gen19610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19611" type="x-p"/> IV. Another expedition against Egypt. From the former he <hi type="italic">returned with great riches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.28">v. 28</reference>), and therefore took the first occasion to invade Egypt again, <hi type="italic">at the time appointed</hi> by the divine Providence, two years after, in the eighth year of his reign, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.29">v. 29</reference>. He shall come <hi type="italic">towards the south.</hi> But this attempt shall not succeed, as the two former did, nor shall he gain his point, as he had done before once and again; for (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.30">v. 30</reference>) <hi type="italic">the ships of Chittim shall come against him,</hi> that is, the navy of the Romans, or only ambassadors from the Roman senate, who came in ships. So Livy and others relate the story which this prophecy refers to. <hi type="italic">He shall be grieved, and return;</hi> for it was a great vexation to him to be forced to yield thus. <div eID="gen19611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19612" type="x-p"/> V. His rage and cruel practices against the Jews. This is that part of his government, or mis-government rather, which is most enlarged upon in this prediction. He grew very proud, insolent, and profane, and, being puffed up with his conquests, bade defiance to Heaven, and trampled upon every thing that was sacred, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">v. 36</reference>, &c. It is plain that St. Paul, in his prophecy of the rise and reign of the man of sin, alludes to this (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2 Thess. ii. 4</reference>), which shows that Antiochus was a type and figure of that enemy, as Babylon also was; but, this being joined in a continued discourse with the foregoing prophecies concerning Antiochus, to me it seems probably that it principally refers to him, and in him had its primary accomplishment, and has reference to the other only by way of accommodation. Antiochus wrote to his own kingdom that every one should leave the gods he had worshipped, and worship such as he ordered, contrary to the practice of all the conquerors that went before him, <reference osisRef="1Macc.1.41-1Macc.1.42">1 Mac. i. 41, 42.</reference> And <hi type="italic">all the heathen agreed according to the commandment of the king;</hi> fond as they were of their gods, they did not think them worth suffering for, but, their gods being idols, it was all alike to them what gods they worshipped. Antiochus did not <hi type="italic">regard any god,</hi> but <hi type="italic">magnified himself above all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">v. 37</reference>. He was so proud that he thought himself above the condition of a mortal man, that he could <hi type="italic">command the waves of the sea, and reach to the stars of heaven,</hi> as his insolence and haughtiness are expressed, <reference osisRef="2Macc.9.8">2 Mac. ix. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Macc.9.10">10</reference>. Thus he carried all before him, <hi type="italic">till the indignation was accomplished</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">v. 36</reference>), till he had run his length, and filled up the measure of his iniquity; for <hi type="italic">that which is determined shall be done,</hi> and nothing more, nothing short. (3.) He shall, contrary to the way of the heathen, disregard the god of his fathers, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.37">v. 37</reference>. Though an affection to the religion of their ancestors was, among the heathen, almost as natural to them as <hi type="italic">the desire of women</hi> (for, if you search through <hi type="italic">the isles of Chittim,</hi> you will not find an instance of a nation that has <hi type="italic">changed its gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.10-Jer.2.11">Jer. ii. 10, 11</reference>), yet Antiochus shall not <hi type="italic">regard the god of his fathers;</hi> he made laws to abolish the religion of his country, and to bring in the idols of the Greeks. And though his predecessors had honoured the God of Israel, and given great gifts to the temple at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Macc.3.2-2Macc.3.3">2 Mac. iii. 2, 3</reference>), he offered the greatest indignities to God and his temple. His not regarding the <hi type="italic">desire of women</hi> may denote his barbarous cruelty (he shall spare no age or sex, no, not the tender ones) or his unnatural lusts, or, in general, his contempt of every thing which men of honour have a concern for, or it might be accomplished in something we meet not with in history. Its being joined to his not <hi type="italic">regarding the god of his fathers</hi> intimates that the idolatries of his country had in them more of the gratifications of the flesh than those of other countries (Lucian has written of the Syrian goddesses), and yet that would not prevail to keep him to them. (4.) He shall set up an unknown god, a new god, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.38">v. 38</reference>. <hi type="italic">In his estate,</hi> in the room of the god of his fathers (Apollo and Diana, deities of pleasure), he shall <hi type="italic">honour the god of forces,</hi> a supposed deity of power, a <hi type="italic">god whom his fathers knew not,</hi> nor worshipped; because he will be thought in wisdom and strength to excel his fathers, he shall <hi type="italic">honour this god with gold, and silver, and precious stones,</hi> thinking nothing too good for the god he has taken a fancy to. This seems to be Jupiter Olympius, known among the Phœnicians by the name of <hi type="italic">Baal-Semen, the lord of heaven,</hi> but never introduced among the Syrians till Antiochus introduced it. Thus shall he do <hi type="italic">in the most strong holds,</hi> in the temple of Jerusalem, which is called <hi type="italic">the sanctuary of strength</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.31">v. 31</reference>), and here the <hi type="italic">fortresses of munitions; there</hi> he shall set up the image of this <hi type="italic">strange god.</hi> Some read it, <hi type="italic">He shall commit the munitions of strength,</hi> or of the most strong God (that is, the city Jerusalem), to <hi type="italic">a strange god;</hi> he put it under the protection and government of Jupiter Olympius. This god he shall not only acknowledge, but shall <hi type="italic">increase with glory,</hi> by setting his image even upon God's altar. And he shall <hi type="italic">cause those</hi> that minister to this idol <hi type="italic">to rule over many,</hi> shall put them into places of power and trust, and they shall <hi type="italic">divide the land for gain,</hi> shall be maintained richly out of the profits of the country. Some by the <hi type="italic">Mahuzzim,</hi> or <hi type="italic">god of forces,</hi> that Antiochus shall worship, understand <hi type="italic">money,</hi> which is said to <hi type="italic">answer all things,</hi> and which is the great idol of worldly people. <div eID="gen19617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19618" type="x-p"/> Now here is very much that is applicable to the <hi type="italic">man of sin;</hi> he <hi type="italic">exalts himself above all that is called god or that is worshipped; magnifies himself above all;</hi> his flatterers call him <hi type="italic">our lord god the pope.</hi> By forbidding marriage, and magnifying the single life, he pretends not to regard the desire of women; and honours the <hi type="italic">god of forces,</hi> the god <hi type="italic">Mahuzzim,</hi> or <hi type="italic">strong holds,</hi> saints and angels, whom his followers take for their protectors, as the heathen did of old their demons; these they make presidents of several countries, &c. These they honour with vast treasures dedicated to them, and therein the learned Mr. Mede thinks that this prophecy was fulfilled, and that it is referred to <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.2">1 Tim. iv. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen19618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19619" type="x-p"/> VI. Here seems to be another expedition into Egypt, or, at least, a struggle with Egypt. The Romans had tied him up from invading Ptolemy, but now that <hi type="italic">king of the south pushes at him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.40">v. 40</reference>), makes an attempt upon some of his territories, where upon Antiochus, the <hi type="italic">king of the north, comes against him like a whirlwind,</hi> with incredible swiftness and fury, <hi type="italic">with chariots, and horses, and many ships,</hi> a great force. He shall <hi type="italic">come through countries, and shall overflow and pass over.</hi> In this flying march <hi type="italic">many countries shall be overthrown by him;</hi> and he shall enter into <hi type="italic">the glorious land,</hi> the land of Israel; it is the same word that is translated <hi type="italic">the pleasant land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">ch. viii. 9</reference>. He shall make dreadful work among the nations thereabout; yet some shall escape his fury, particularly Edom and Moab, and <hi type="italic">the chief of the children of Ammon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">v. 41</reference>. He did not put these countries under contribution, because they had joined with him against the Jews. But especially the land of Egypt <hi type="italic">shall not escape,</hi> but he will quite beggar that, so bare will he strip it. This some reckon his fourth and last expedition against Egypt, in the tenth or eleventh year of his reign, under pretence of assisting the younger brother of Ptolemæus Philometer against him. We read not of any great slaughter made in this expedition, but great plunder; for, it should seem, that was what he came for: <hi type="italic">He shall have power over the treasures of gold and silver, and all the precious things of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.43">v. 43</reference>. Polybius, in Athenæus, relates that Antiochus, having got together abundance of wealth, by spoiling young Philometer, and breaking league with him, and by the contributions of his friends, bestowed a vast deal upon a triumph, in imitation of Paulus Æmilius, and describes the extravagance of it; here we are told how he got that money which he spent so profusely. Notice is here taken likewise of the use he made of the Lybians and Ethiopians, who bordered upon Egypt; they <hi type="italic">were at his steps;</hi> he had them at his foot, had them at his beck, and they made inroads upon Egypt to serve him. <div eID="gen19619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19620" type="x-p"/> VII. Here is a prediction of the fall and ruin of Antiochus, as before (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">ch. viii. 25</reference>), when he is in the height of his honour, flushed with victory, and laden with spoils, tidings <hi type="italic">out of the east</hi> and <hi type="italic">out of the north</hi> (out of the north-east) shall trouble him, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.44">v. 44</reference>. Or, He shall have intelligence, both from the eastern and northern parts, that the king of Parthia is invading his kingdom. This obliged him to drop the enterprises he had in hand, and to go against the Persians and Parthians that were revolting from him; and this <hi type="italic">vexed</hi> him, for now he thought utterly to ruin and extirpate the Jewish nation, when that expedition called him off, in which he perished. This is explained by a passage in Tacitus (though an impious one) where he commends Antiochus for his attempt to <hi type="italic">take away the superstition of the Jews,</hi> and <hi type="italic">bring in the manners of the Greeks,</hi> among them (<hi type="italic">ut teterrimam gentem in melius mutaret—to meliorate an odious nation</hi>), and laments that he was hindered from accomplishing it by the Parthian war. Now here is, 1. The last effort of his rage against the Jews. When he finds himself perplexed and embarrassed in his affairs he shall <hi type="italic">go forth with great fury to destroy and utterly to make away many,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.11.44">v. 44</reference>. The story of this we have <reference osisRef="1Macc.3.27">1 Mac. iii. 27</reference>, &c., what a rage Antiochus was in when he heard of the successes of Judas Maccabæus, and the orders he gave to Lysias to destroy Jerusalem. Then <hi type="italic">he planted the tabernacles of his palace,</hi> or <hi type="italic">tents of his court, between the seas,</hi> between the Great Sea and the Dead Sea. He set up his royal pavilion at Emmaus near Jerusalem, in token that, though he could not be present himself, yet he gave full power to his captains to prosecute the war against the Jews with the utmost rigour. He placed his tent there, as if he had taken possession <hi type="italic">of the glorious holy mountain</hi> and called it <hi type="italic">his own.</hi> Note, When impiety grows very impudent we may see its ruin near. 2. His exit: <hi type="italic">He shall come to his end and none shall help him;</hi> God shall cut him off in the midst of his days and none shall be able to prevent his fall. This is the same with that which was foretold <reference osisRef="Dan.8.35">ch. viii. 25</reference> (<hi type="italic">He shall be broken without hand</hi>), where we took a view of his miserable end. Note, When God's time shall come to bring proud oppressors to their end none shall be able to help them, nor perhaps inclined to help them; for those that covet to be feared by all when they are in their grandeur, when they come to be in distress will find themselves loved by none; none will lend them so much as a hand or a prayer to help them; and, if the Lord do not help, who shall? <div eID="gen19620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19621" type="x-p"/> Of the kings that came after Antiochus nothing is here prophesied, for that was the most malicious mischievous enemy to the church, that was a type of the son of perdition, whom the Lord shall consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy with the brightness of his coming, and none shall help him.  <chapter eID="Dan.11"/> <div eID="gen19621" type="x-p"/>

entries.4be34de21624dd675ad21f8103a3951d41251679: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12184"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.11.1-Dan.11.45">Da 11:1-45</reference>. This chapter is an enlargement of the eighth: The Overthrow of Persia by Grecia: The Four Divisions of Alexander's Kingdom:</title> <div sID="gen22101" type="x-p"/> Conflicts between the Kings of the South and of the North, the Ptolemies and Seleucidæ: Antiochus Epiphanes.<div eID="gen22101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12184"/><hi type="bold">1. I--</hi>the angel (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.18">Da 10:18</reference>).<div eID="gen22102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first year of Darius--</hi>Cyaxares II; the year of the conquest of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.31">Da 5:31</reference>). Cyrus, who wielded the real power, though in name subordinate to Darius, in that year promulgated the edict for the restoration of the Jews, which Daniel was at the time praying for (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.1">Da 9:1</reference>, 2, 21, 23).<div eID="gen22103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stood--</hi>implying promptness in helping (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.16">Psa 94:16</reference>).<div eID="gen22104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strengthen him--</hi>namely, Michael; even as Michael (<reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Da 10:21</reference>, "strengtheneth himself with me") helped the angel, both joining their powers in behalf of Israel [Rosenmuller]. Or, Darius, the angel "confirming him" in his purpose of kindness to Israel. <div eID="gen22105" type="x-p"/>
entries.35bf3c70e94d2fb810e787b9cfaa616d2f015e37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12185"/><div sID="gen22106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12185"/><hi type="bold">2. three kings in Persia--</hi>Cambyses, Pseudo-Smerdis, and Darius Hystaspes. (Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, and Darius, in <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.6">Ezr 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.24">7, 24</reference>). The Ahasuerus of Esther (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.9.1">Da 9:1</reference>) is identified with Xerxes, both in Greek history and in Scripture, appearing proud, self-willed, careless of contravening Persian customs, amorous, facile, and changeable (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.2">Da 11:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fourth ... riches ... against ... Grecia--</hi>Xerxes, whose riches were proverbial. Persia reached its climax and showed its greatest power in his invasion of Greece, 480 B.C. After his overthrow at Salamis, Persia is viewed as politically dead, though it had an existence. Therefore, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.3">Da 11:3</reference>, without noticing Xerxes' successors, proceeds at once to Alexander, under whom, first, the third world kingdom, Grecia, reached its culmination, and assumed an importance as to the people of God.<div eID="gen22107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stir up all--</hi>Four years were spent in gathering his army out of all parts of his vast empire, amounting to two millions six hundred and forty-one thousand men. [Prideaux, Connexion, 1.4. l. 410]. <div eID="gen22108" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac001f205e1b4576df2d8acd6e18947edb8392f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12186"/><div sID="gen22109" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12186"/><hi type="bold">3. mighty king ... do according to his will--</hi>answering to the he-goat's "notable horn" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.6">Da 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.21">7, 21</reference>). Alexander invaded Persia 334 B.C., to avenge the wrongs of Greece on Persia for Xerxes' past invasion (as Alexander said in a letter to Darius Codomanus, Arrian, Alexander. 2.14.7). <div eID="gen22109" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6db0e9608a749f27fadd4c4e23405974c477c44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12187"/><div sID="gen22110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12187"/><hi type="bold">4. kingdom ... divided toward ... four winds--</hi>the fourfold division of Alexander's kingdom at his death (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.8">Da 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.22">22</reference>), after the battle of Ipsus, 301 B.C.<div eID="gen22110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not to his posterity--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Dan.8.8">Da 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.22">Da 8:22</reference>).<div eID="gen22111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor according to his dominion--</hi>None of his successors had so wide a dominion as Alexander himself.<div eID="gen22112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">others besides those--</hi>besides Alexander's sons, Hercules by Barsine, Darius' daughter, and Alexander by Roxana, who were both slain [Maurer]. Rather, besides the four successors to the four chief divisions of the empire, there will be other lesser chiefs who shall appropriate smaller fragments of the Macedonian empire [Jerome]. <div eID="gen22113" type="x-p"/>
entries.2eaf65626be4c17223ce21b618c734b8503ffce3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12188"/><div sID="gen22114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12188"/>5. Here the prophet leaves Asia and Greece and takes up Egypt and Syria, these being in continual conflict under Alexander's successors, entailing misery on Judea, which lay between the two. Holy Scripture handles external history only so far as it is connected with God's people, Israel [Jerome]. Tregelles puts a chasm between the fourth and fifth verses, making the transition to the final Antichrist here, answering to the chasm (in his view) at <reference osisRef="Dan.8.22">Da 8:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">23</reference>.<div eID="gen22114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king of ... south--</hi>literally, "of midday": Egypt (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.8">Da 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.42">42</reference>), Ptolemy Soter, son of Lagus. He took the title "king," whereas Lagus was but "governor."<div eID="gen22115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one of his princes--</hi>Seleucus, at first a satrap of Ptolemy Lagus, but from 312 B.C. king of the largest empire after that of Alexander (Syria, Babylon, Media, &c.), and called therefore Nicator, that is, "conqueror." Connect the words thus, "And one of his (Ptolemy's) princes, even he (Seleucus) shall be strong above him" (above Ptolemy, his former master). <div eID="gen22116" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d4d6b9e08f3c6c6d4c5aae44e5dd86342be795d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12189"/><div sID="gen22117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12189"/><hi type="bold">6. in ... end of years--</hi>when the predicted time shall be consummated (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.13">Da 11:13</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.17">Da 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.13">12:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king's daughter of the south--</hi>Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy Philadelphus of Egypt. The latter, in order to end his war with Antiochus Theus, "king of the north" (literally, "midnight": the prophetical phrase for the region whence came affliction to Israel, <reference osisRef="Jer.1.13-Jer.1.15">Jr 1:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.20">Joe 2:20</reference>), that is, Syria, gave Berenice to Antiochus, who thereupon divorced his former wife, Laodice, and disinherited her son, Seleucus Callinicus. The designation, "king of the north" and "of the south," is given in relation to Judea, as the standpoint. Egypt is mentioned by name (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.8">Da 11:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.42">42</reference>), though Syria is not; because the former was in Daniel's time a flourishing kingdom, whereas Syria was then a mere dependency of Assyria and Babylon: an undesigned proof of the genuineness of the Book of Daniel.<div eID="gen22118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">agreement--</hi>literally, "rights," that is, to put things to rights between the belligerents.<div eID="gen22119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she shall not retain the power of the arm--</hi>She shall not be able to effect the purpose of the alliance, namely, that she should be the mainstay of peace. Ptolemy having died, Antiochus took back Laodice, who then poisoned him, and caused Berenice and her son to be put to death, and raised her own son, Seleucus Nicator, to the throne.<div eID="gen22120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither shall he stand--</hi>The king of Egypt shall not gain his point of setting his line on the throne of Syria.<div eID="gen22121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his arm--</hi>that on which he relied. Berenice and her offspring.<div eID="gen22122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they that brought her--</hi>her attendants from Egypt.<div eID="gen22123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that begat her--</hi>rather as Margin, "the child whom she brought forth" [Ewald]. If English Version (which Maurer approves) be retained, as Ptolemy died a natural death, "given up" is not in his case, as in Berenice's, to be understood of giving up to death, but in a general sense, of his plan proving abortive.<div eID="gen22124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that strengthened her in these times--</hi>Antiochus Theus, who is to attach himself to her (having divorced Laodice) at the times predicted [Gejer]. <div eID="gen22125" type="x-p"/>
entries.337bfc7548cb38aa8a3c925129365a5792f3cec6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12190"/><div sID="gen22126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12190"/><hi type="bold">7. a branch of her roots ... in his estate--</hi>Ptolemy Euergetes, brother of Berenice, succeeding in the place (Margin) of Philadelphus, avenged her death by overrunning Syria, even to the Euphrates.<div eID="gen22126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deal against them--</hi>He shall deal with the Syrians at his own pleasure. He slew Laodice. <div eID="gen22127" type="x-p"/>
entries.854acf426ad075ffc60763e365546a4f0bad9d31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12191"/><div sID="gen22128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12191"/><hi type="bold">8. carry ... into Egypt their gods, &c.--</hi>Ptolemy, on hearing of a sedition in Egypt, returned with forty thousand talents of silver, precious vessels, and twenty-four hundred images, including Egyptian idols, which Cambyses had carried from Egypt into Persia. The idolatrous Egyptians were so gratified, that they named him Euergetes, or "benefactor."<div eID="gen22128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continue more years--</hi>Ptolemy survived Seleucus four years, reigning in all forty-six years. Maurer translates, "Then he for several years shall desist from (contending with) the king of the north" (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.11.9">Da 11:9</reference>). <div eID="gen22129" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfb708bf054ee11eb0c24ab4a2f245dee95f9a55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12192"/><div sID="gen22130" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12192"/><hi type="bold">9. come into his kingdom--</hi>Egypt: not only with impunity, but with great spoil. <div eID="gen22130" type="x-p"/>
entries.39c0e4396ee2a950e7725217a54ce1e63514b66d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12193"/><div sID="gen22131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12193"/><hi type="bold">10. his sons--</hi>the two sons of the king of the north, Seleucus Callinicus, upon his death by a fall from his horse, namely, Seleucus Ceraunus and Antiochus the Great.<div eID="gen22131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one shall ... come--</hi>Ceraunus having died, Antiochus alone prosecuted the war with Ptolemy Philopater, Euergetes' son, until he had recovered all the parts of Syria subjugated by Euergetes.<div eID="gen22132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pass through--</hi>like an "overflowing" torrent (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.22">Da 11:22</reference>, 26, 40; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Is 8:8</reference>). Antiochus penetrated to Dura (near Cæsarea), where he gave Ptolemy a four months' truce.<div eID="gen22133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return--</hi>renew the war at the expiration of the truce (so <reference osisRef="Dan.11.13">Da 11:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even to his fortress--</hi>Ptolemy's; Raphia, a border-fortress of Egypt against incursions by way of Edom and Arabia-Petræa, near Gaza; here Antiochus was vanquished. <div eID="gen22135" type="x-p"/>
entries.0038cd52d463676a0bbf4986d92496c468755327: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12194"/><div sID="gen22136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12194"/><hi type="bold">11. the king of the south ... moved with choler--</hi>at so great losses, Syria having been wrested from him, and his own kingdom imperilled, though otherwise an indolent man, to which his disasters were owing, as also to the odium of his subjects against him for having murdered his father, mother, and brother, whence in irony they called him Philopater, "father-lover."<div eID="gen22136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall set forth a great multitude--</hi>Antiochus, king of Syria, whose force was seventy thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry.<div eID="gen22137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but ... multitude ... given into his hand--</hi>into Ptolemy's hands; ten thousand of Antiochus' army were slain, and four thousand made captives. <div eID="gen22138" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c4ea9aade7e723d3b1fad358137dbd6bffaab9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12195"/><div sID="gen22139" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12195"/><hi type="bold">12. when he hath taken away--</hi>that is, subdued "the multitude" of Antiochus.<div eID="gen22139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22140" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart ... lifted up--</hi>instead of following up his victory by making himself master of the whole of Syria, as he might, he made peace with Antiochus, and gave himself up to licentiousness [Polybius, 87; Justin, 30.4], and profaned the temple of God by entering the holy place [Grotius].<div eID="gen22140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not be strengthened by it--</hi>He shall lose the power gained by his victory through his luxurious indolence. <div eID="gen22141" type="x-p"/>
entries.5966b31a75ed3856cf210283002af1a4167baa35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12196"/><div sID="gen22142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12196"/><hi type="bold">13. return--</hi>renew the war.<div eID="gen22142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22143" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after certain years--</hi>fourteen years after his defeat at Raphia. Antiochus, after successful campaigns against Persia and India, made war with Ptolemy Epiphanes, son of Philopater, a mere child. <div eID="gen22143" type="x-p"/>
entries.b09616c181825c6057410261cf4ecebe8442e228: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12197"/><div sID="gen22144" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12197"/><hi type="bold">14. many stand up against the king of the south--</hi>Philip, king of Macedon, and rebels in Egypt itself, combined with Antiochus against Ptolemy.<div eID="gen22144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">robbers of thy people--</hi>that is, factious men of the Jews shall exalt themselves, so as to revolt from Ptolemy, and join themselves to Antiochus; the Jews helped Antiochus' army with provisions, when on his return from Egypt he besieged the Egyptian garrison left in Jerusalem [Josephus, Antiquities, 12:3.3].<div eID="gen22145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to establish the vision--</hi>Those turbulent Jews unconsciously shall help to fulfil the purpose of God, as to the trials which await Judea, according to this vision.<div eID="gen22146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but they shall fall--</hi>Though helping to fulfil the vision, they shall fail in their aim, of making Judea independent. <div eID="gen22147" type="x-p"/>
entries.76485a601b09915b94c6d5936650840ba12cfc52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12198"/><div sID="gen22148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12198"/><hi type="bold">15. king of ... north--</hi>Antiochus the Great.<div eID="gen22148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take ... fenced cities--</hi>Scopas, the Egyptian general, met Antiochus at Paneas, near the sources of the Jordan, and was defeated, and fled to Sidon, a strongly "fenced city," where he was forced to surrender.<div eID="gen22149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chosen people--</hi>Egypt's choicest army was sent under Eropus, Menocles, and Damoxenus, to deliver Scopas, but in vain [Jerome]. <div eID="gen22150" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b6515672e68572d4c3b0fac00af1ad14b5cbc80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12199"/><div sID="gen22151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12199"/><hi type="bold">16. he that cometh against him--</hi>Antiochus coming against Ptolemy Epiphanes.<div eID="gen22151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glorious land--</hi>Judea (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">Da 11:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.45">45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen22152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by his hand shall be consumed--</hi>literally, "perfected," that is, completely brought under his sway. Josephus [Antiquities, 12:3.3] shows that the meaning is not, that the Jews should be utterly consumed: for Antiochus favored them for taking his part against Ptolemy, but that their land should be subjected to him [Lengkerke]. Grotius translates, "shall be perfected by him," that is, shall flourish under him. English Version gives a good sense; namely, that Judea was much "consumed" or "desolated" by being the arena of conflict between the combatants, Syria and Egypt. Tregelles refers (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">Da 11:14</reference>), "robbers of thy people," to the Gentiles, once oppressors, attempting to restore the Jews to their land by mere human effort, whereas this is to be effected only by divine interposition: their attempt is frustrated (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Da 11:16</reference>) by the wilful king, who makes Judea the scene of his military operations. <div eID="gen22153" type="x-p"/>
entries.136bad94b95bf24ffcc151c7e70214b7e5d24ce2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12200"/><div sID="gen22154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12200"/><hi type="bold">17. set his face--</hi>purpose steadfastly. Antiochus purpose was, however, turned from open assault to wile, by his war with the Romans in his endeavor to extend his kingdom to the limits it had under Seleucus Nicator.<div eID="gen22154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upright one--</hi>Jasher, or Jeshurun (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.2">Is 44:2</reference>); the epithet applied by the Hebrews to their nation. It is here used not in praise; for in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">Da 11:14</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">Da 11:14</reference>) they are called "robbers," or "men of violence, factious": it is the general designation of Israel, as having God for their God. Probably it is used to rebuke those who ought to have been God's "upright ones" for confederating with godless heathen in acts of violence (the contrast to the term in <reference osisRef="Dan.11.14">Da 11:14</reference> favors this).<div eID="gen22155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thus shall he do--</hi>Instead of at once invading Ptolemy's country with his "whole strength," he prepares his way for doing so by the following plan: he gives to Ptolemy Epiphanes his daughter Cleopatra in marriage, promising Coelo-Syria and Judea as a dowry, thus securing his neutrality in the war with Rome: he hoped through his daughter to obtain Syria, Cilicia, and Lycia, and even Egypt itself at last; but Cleopatra favored her husband rather than her father, and so defeated his scheme [Jerome]. "She shall not stand on his side." <div eID="gen22156" type="x-p"/>
entries.958015e1b3d73c9086eb732ff8403e64818c871b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12201"/><div sID="gen22157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12201"/><hi type="bold">18. isles--</hi>He "took many" of the isles in the Ægean in his war with the Romans, and crossed the Hellespont.<div eID="gen22157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prince for his own behalf shall cause the reproach ... to cease--</hi>Lucius Scipio Asiaticus, the Roman general, by routing Antiochus at Magnesia (190 B.C.), caused the reproach which he offered Rome by inflicting injuries on Rome's allies, to cease. He did it for his own glory.<div eID="gen22158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without his own reproach--</hi>with untarnished reputation. <div eID="gen22159" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c62c2e8e669ba830d77e7f2b796e637dc323751: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12202"/><div sID="gen22160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12202"/><hi type="bold">19. Then he shall turn ... toward ... his own land--</hi>Compelled by Rome to relinquish all his territory west of the Taurus, and defray the expenses of the war, he garrisoned the cities left to him.<div eID="gen22160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stumble ... not be found--</hi>Attempting to plunder the temple of Jupiter at Elymais by night, whether through avarice, or the want of money to pay the tribute imposed by Rome (a thousand talents), he was slain with his soldiers in an insurrection of the inhabitants [Justin, 32.2]. <div eID="gen22161" type="x-p"/>
entries.51365e76d4b2137f382bc09bda725b72fe0951de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12203"/><div sID="gen22162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12203"/><hi type="bold">20. in his estate--</hi>in Antiochus' stead: his successor, Seleucus Philopater, his son.<div eID="gen22162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the glory of the kingdom--</hi>that is, inheriting it by hereditary right. Maurer translates, "one who shall cause the tax gatherer (Heliodorus) to pass through the glory of the kingdom," that is, Judea, "the glorious land" (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">Da 11:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.41">41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>). Simon, a Benjamite, in spite against Onias III, the high priest, gave information of the treasures in the Jewish temple; and Seleucus having reunited to Syria Coelo-Syria and Palestine, the dowry formerly given by Antiochus the Great to Cleopatra, Ptolemy's wife, sent Heliodorus to Jerusalem to plunder the temple. This is narrated in 2 Maccabees 3:4, &c. Contrast <reference osisRef="Zech.9.8">Zec 9:8</reference>, "No oppressor shall pass through ... any more."<div eID="gen22163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">within few days ... destroyed--</hi>after a reign of twelve years, which were "few" compared with the thirty-seven years of Antiochus' reign. Heliodorus, the instrument of Seleucus' sacrilege, was made by God the instrument of his punishment. Seeking the crown, in the absence at Rome of Seleucus' only son and heir, Demetrius, he poisoned Seleucus. But Antiochus Epiphanes, Seleucus' brother, by the help of Eumenes, king of Pergamos, succeeded to the throne, 175 B.C.<div eID="gen22164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither in anger, nor in battle--</hi>not in a popular outbreak, nor in open battle. <div eID="gen22165" type="x-p"/>
entries.b84b9fe7348638d73a1b9230ffb5877d8a4a6427: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12204"/><div sID="gen22166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12204"/><hi type="bold">21. vile--</hi>Antiochus called Epiphanes, that is, "the illustrious," for vindicating the claims of the royal line against Heliodorus, was nicknamed, by a play of sounds, Epimanes, that is, "the madman," for his mad freaks beneath the dignity of a king. He would carouse with the lowest of the people, bathe with them in the public baths, and foolishly jest and throw stones at passers-by [Polybius, 26.10]. Hence, as also for his crafty supplanting of Demetrius, the rightful heir, from the throne, he is termed "vile."<div eID="gen22166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall not give ... kingdom: but ... by flatteries--</hi>The nation shall not, by a public act, confer the kingdom on him, but he shall obtain it by artifice, "flattering" Eumenes and Attalus of Pergamos to help him, and, as he had seen candidates at Rome doing, canvassing the Syrian people high and low, one by one, with embraces [Livy, 41.20]. <div eID="gen22167" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc88767562f82244bcf747be1112c31e205f05bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12205"/><div sID="gen22168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12205"/><hi type="bold">22. shall they be overflown ... before him--</hi>Antiochus Epiphanes shall invade Egypt with overwhelming forces.<div eID="gen22168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prince of the covenant--</hi>Ptolemy Philometer, the son of Cleopatra, Antiochus' sister, who was joined in covenant with him. Ptolemy's guardians, while he was a boy, sought to recover from Epiphanes Coelo-Syria and Palestine, which had been promised by Antiochus the Great as Cleopatra's dowry in marrying Ptolemy Epiphanes. Hence arose the war. Philometer's generals were vanquished, and Pelusium, the key of Egypt, taken by Antiochus, 171 B.C. <div eID="gen22169" type="x-p"/>
entries.a56f6daa35c7fc8f2e95496287c82fae3f15b4d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12206"/><div sID="gen22170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12206"/>23. Tregelles notes three divisions in the history of the "vile person," which is continued to the end of the chapter: (1) His rise (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.21">Da 11:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.22">22</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2</reference>) The time from his making the covenant to the taking away of the daily sacrifice and setting up of the abomination of desolation (Da 11:23-31). (3) His career of blasphemy, to his destruction (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.32-Dan.11.45">Da 11:32-45</reference>); the latter two periods answering to the "week" of years of his "covenant with many" (namely, in Israel) (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>), and the last being the closing half week of the ninth chapter. But the context so accurately agrees with the relations of Antiochus to Ptolemy that the primary reference seems to be to the "league" between them. Antitypically, Antichrist's relations towards Israel are probably delineated. Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.8.11">Da 8:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">25</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Dan.11.22">Da 11:22</reference> here, "prince of the covenant."<div eID="gen22170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work deceitfully--</hi>Feigning friendship to young Ptolemy, as if he wished to order his kingdom for him, he took possession of Memphis and all Egypt ("the fattest places," <reference osisRef="Dan.11.34">Da 11:34</reference>) as far as Alexandria.<div eID="gen22171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a small people--</hi>At first, to throw off suspicion, his forces were small. <div eID="gen22172" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ab98fc97ad83ae2f779f9a14d2127c6f780b790: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12207"/><div sID="gen22173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12207"/><hi type="bold">24. peaceably--</hi>literally, "unexpectedly"; under the guise of friendship he seized Ptolemy Philometer.<div eID="gen22173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall do that which his fathers have not done--</hi>His predecessors, kings of Syria, had always coveted Egypt, but in vain: he alone made himself master of it.<div eID="gen22174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scatter among them ... prey--</hi>among his followers (1 Maccabees 1:19).<div eID="gen22175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forecast his devices against ... strongholds--</hi>He shall form a studied scheme for making himself master of the Egyptian fortresses. He gained them all except Alexandria, which successfully resisted him. Retaining to himself Pelusium, he retired to Judea, where, in revenge for the joy shown by the Jews at the report of his death, which led them to a revolt, he subdued Jerusalem by storm or stratagem.<div eID="gen22176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a time--</hi>His rage shall not be for ever; it is but for a time limited by God. Calvin makes "for a time" in antithesis to "unexpectedly," in the beginning of the verse. He suddenly mastered the weaker cities: he had to "forecast his plans" more gradually ("for a time") as to how to gain the stronger fortresses. <div eID="gen22177" type="x-p"/>
entries.55976ce00d3a8c216d91a59288089526af1336a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12208"/><div sID="gen22178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12208"/>25. A fuller detail of what was summarily stated (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.22-Dan.11.24">Da 11:22-24</reference>). This is the first of Antiochus' three (<reference osisRef="Dan.11.29">Da 11:29</reference>) open invasions of Egypt.<div eID="gen22178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against the king of the south--</hi>against Ptolemy Philometer.
